title: First Mass, or first in years
hook: the hardest part is walking through the door; nobody at the door asks where you've been

segments.voice: Yesterday, communio sanctorum, the communion of saints. Your line was so great a cloud of witnesses. Now Camp Three: the practices.

A church parking lot, ten minutes before Sunday Mass. Someone sits in a car with the engine off, watching families cross the lot. They haven't been inside in eleven years. Or they've never been inside at all, and a friend said, just come once. Their hands are a little sweaty. What if everyone can tell? What if I stand up at the wrong time? People who've made that walk say it afterward: the hardest part was the door.
screen: `TEN MINUTES BEFORE MASS.` → `ELEVEN YEARS, OR NEVER.` → `THE HARDEST PART IS THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Parish comes from a Greek word, paroikia, for people living away from home: neighbors who are also, in a sense, strangers. The first letter of Peter calls Christians, in the Douay-Rheims, "strangers and pilgrims." So a parish was never a club for people who already belong. It's a house full of people on the way. People walk in for a funeral or a wedding, after a hard year, for a partner, or out of plain curiosity. And people step away for all kinds of reasons: some stopped believing, some were hurt, some drifted, or were never really taught. Nobody at the door asks which. You're not behind. What happens inside? Sit anywhere; the back is fine. There's usually a book or a card in the pew with the words. Stand, sit and kneel when the people around you do. Nobody is grading. At Communion, Catholics who are ready go up to receive. Anyone who isn't, a guest, someone on the way to becoming Catholic, a Catholic who isn't ready yet, can stay in the pew, or in many parishes come up with arms crossed over the chest for a blessing. Both are normal. When you want a next step, someone coming back can talk to a priest, and go to confession when they're ready; that's a whole lesson later on. Adults who want to become Catholic go through a process many parishes now call OCIA, the Order of Christian Initiation of Adults; it used to be called RCIA. Some lifelong Catholics sit in on it as a refresher. And the line people hear over and over, from the pew next to them, is two words: welcome home.
screen: `PARISH: STRANGERS AND PILGRIMS.` · `MANY REASONS TO LEAVE, AND TO COME.` · `SIT, STAND, KNEEL WITH EVERYONE.` · `ARMS CROSSED FOR A BLESSING.`

segments.voice: Picture a church you know, or one you've driven past: your hand on the door handle, the small hush as it closes behind you, a seat near the back. Notice the light and the quiet; nobody turns around. Sit there a while and let it be all right that you came, and if you pray, say so, in a word or two.
Parish. From the Greek for people living away from home: the local church, open to whoever walks in.
Your line: welcome home. Whether it's your first Mass or your first in years, that's what the door is for. Tomorrow, the water just inside it.

screen: `DAY 97 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: HOLY WATER AT THE DOOR.`

howItsDone: Anyone may attend Mass. Visitors and returning Catholics sit where they like and follow the people around them; those not receiving Communion stay in the pew or, in many parishes, come forward with arms crossed for a blessing. Adults who wish to become Catholic join their parish's OCIA (formerly RCIA).

fork.setup: Communion time. you're a guest, or a Catholic who isn't ready to receive yet. your whole row stands up. what do you do?
options: go up and receive, so nobody notices.
stay seated, or go up with arms crossed for a blessing.
fork.reveal: either one is completely normal. people let others past all the time, and in many parishes the blessing line is just part of the line.

original.note: Greek: a sojourning, living as a neighbor away from home. Through Latin parochia it became parish.

trapdoor: what you thought: a parish is the church building, or the club of people who belong there.
what it means: the local community of Catholics, open to anyone who walks in, whether it's their first Mass or their first in years.

what a scholar hears: paroikia, from paroikos, a resident alien or sojourner. 1 Peter 2:11 calls Christians paroikous, "strangers and pilgrims"; the word for exiles became the word for the local church.
